sermon:
## The Kingdom Has Come Near: The Beginning of the Gospel (Mark 1:1-45)
*Mark opens with a verdict already rendered, and a wilderness that will not let you keep your distance*

**Text:** Mark 1:1-45 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 40:3; Malachi 3:1; Isaiah 64:1; Daniel 7:13-14; Leviticus 13:45-46; 2 Corinthians 5:20

Every other Gospel gives you a runway. Matthew builds a genealogy, Luke sets a manger, John reaches back before the world was made. Mark gives you none of it. He opens the way a man opens a door he intends to walk through without stopping — and he has already decided what he thinks of you before you sit down.

We live now on the far side of Christendom, in a culture that kept the word *gospel* and threw away its edge. It became branding. It became a genre of music and a tone of voice. Mark uses the word once, in the first line, and means something a Roman would have recognized: *euangelion*, the imperial announcement carried through the provinces that a new emperor had taken the throne and the world had changed whether you consented or not. That is the register. Not an invitation to a religion. Not a self-improvement program with a Galilean spokesman. A regime change already underway, announced to a world that did not vote for it.

### I. The Announcement Before the Argument (Mark 1:1-8)

"The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." (Mark 1:1)

There is no verb. Mark does not say *here begins* or *let me tell you.* He drops the title of a book that is also a verdict and moves on. *Christos* — the anointed king, the one Israel had waited on for centuries. *Huios Theou* — Son of God, the phrase Rome stamped on its coins under Caesar's face and read aloud in its temples. Mark takes the empire's own vocabulary, the language of the man who ruled the known world, and hands it to a carpenter from a town so unremarkable that later, in John's Gospel, a man will ask whether anything good can come out of it.

Then Mark does the one thing his whole book will keep doing: he sends you backward before he lets you go forward. He quotes Isaiah 40 and Malachi 3 together — the voice crying in the wilderness, the messenger who prepares the way of the Lord. This is not decoration. Mark is telling you that the thing arriving in verse nine has been arriving for seven centuries, that the wire was laid long before the current ran through it, and that if you thought the story started with John in the desert, you started too late. The full arc is the point. The proximate cause is never where he lets you begin.

- **A. The wilderness is the point, not the setting.** John does not preach in Jerusalem, where the crowds and the temple and the power were. He preaches where Israel was formed, where the covenant was cut, where a people learned across forty years that they could not feed themselves. The crowds have to leave the city to hear him. Repentance always costs a walk out of the place you built for yourself, and Mark makes the geography carry the theology.
- **B. John reduces himself on purpose.** "I have baptized you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit." (Mark 1:8) The most sought-after preacher in the region says he is not worthy to stoop down and untie a sandal. That is not false modesty performed for a crowd. That is a man who knows the difference between the messenger and the message, a distinction the modern pulpit — mine included — loses the moment a platform grows large enough to be mistaken for the kingdom it was supposed to point past.

### II. The Heavens Torn and the Wilderness Won (Mark 1:9-13)

Jesus comes up out of the water and Mark says the heavens were *torn open* — *schizō*, ripped, the same violent word he will use exactly once more, at the very end, when the temple curtain is torn from top to bottom the moment Jesus dies. Mark bookends his Gospel with two tearings. The sky at the baptism, the veil at the cross. Isaiah had cried on behalf of a people in exile, "Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down." (Isaiah 64:1) Mark answers the ancient prayer in his fourth verse: he did. The rending is not gentle. God does not open a door politely and wait to be invited through. He tears the roof off the world.

And the voice speaks — "You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased." (Mark 1:11) — before Jesus has preached a sermon, healed a leper, or gathered a single disciple. The approval comes before the achievement. The Father is pleased with a Son who has not yet, by the world's accounting, done anything. Then the Spirit, the same Spirit that just descended like a dove, immediately *drives* him — Mark's word is *ekballō*, the word he uses everywhere else for casting out a demon — into the wilderness with the wild animals and Satan. The beloved Son is not spared the desert. He is thrown into it by the love that named him.

- **A. Sonship is not a reward for the resistance; it is the ground of it.** Jesus enters the temptation already beloved, already approved, already secure. He does not fight for the Father's approval. He fights from it. Every counterfeit gospel reverses that order and sells you a sonship you have to earn by performance, and a people trying to earn what has already been given to them will always break in the wilderness.
- **B. Where the first Israel failed forty years, this Son holds forty days.** Mark, unlike Matthew and Luke, gives us no dialogue with the tempter, no three exchanges, no quoted Scripture. He does not tell you what was said. He tells you it happened and that the angels ministered to him. Sometimes the whole record of a hard-won victory is just the fact that the man walked back out of the desert still the Son the Father named.

### III. Everyone Recognizes Him But the People Who Want Only the Cure (Mark 1:14-45)

Here is the strange thing Mark makes you notice, and it will govern the rest of the book. The demons know exactly who Jesus is. "I know who you are — the Holy One of God." (Mark 1:24) The unclean spirit in the Capernaum synagogue has sharper Christology than the entire crowd. It confesses the truth and hates it. Meanwhile the people who fill Simon Peter's house until there is no room, not even at the door, want one thing: the miracle. By morning "everyone is looking for you" (Mark 1:37), and Jesus — who could have owned that town by noon, who could have built the whole movement on the momentum of a single successful Sabbath — has already slipped out to a desolate place to pray, and then says the sentence that should stop every church-growth strategy cold: "Let us go on to the next towns, that I may preach there also, for that is why I came out." (Mark 1:38)

Not for the crowd. For the preaching. He walks away from his own success on the second day of his public ministry, before the applause has even finished.

I have to be honest about which side of that door I am usually standing on. I have wanted the results Jesus refused. I have measured a Sunday by the room and not the repentance, and I have called it faithfulness because the room was full. The crowd at Capernaum was not evil. They were sick, and he was healing, and they wanted more healing — who would not? But wanting the gifts is not the same as wanting the Giver, and wanting the cure is not the same as wanting the King. Mark will spend fifteen chapters pulling those two hungers apart until, at a cross outside Jerusalem, only one of them is left standing.

Consider the leper, where the chapter lands. Under the law of Leviticus, uncleanness moved by touch, and it moved in one direction only: the leper made others unclean, never the reverse. He had to live outside the camp, tear his clothes, and cry "Unclean, unclean" so no one would come near. (Leviticus 13:45-46) Everyone in that culture knew which way the defilement flowed. And Jesus, "moved with pity, stretched out his hand and touched him." (Mark 1:41) The wrong direction. The unclean man should have made Jesus unclean. Instead the leper walks away clean. That single reversed touch is the entire gospel in one gesture — holiness that runs uphill, contagious the wrong way, healing what it touches instead of catching what it touched. In the year 251, when a plague tore through the Roman empire and the healthy fled the cities to save themselves, it was the Christians who stayed to nurse the dying, and the pagan world could not account for it. Bishop Dionysius of Alexandria wrote of believers who "drew to themselves the sickness of their neighbors" and died in their place. They had learned the direction of the current from a leper on a road in Galilee.

- **A. The demons confess and the crowd consumes.** Right doctrine and no allegiance is the oldest religion there is. James says the demons believe, and shudder. Capernaum believed enough to line up at the door and not enough to leave the door and follow. A city can affirm every true thing about Jesus and still only want him for what he dispenses.
- **B. The cleansed leper cannot stay quiet, and it costs Jesus the towns.** Jesus tells him to say nothing, and he tells everyone, and now Jesus "could no longer openly enter a town, but was out in desolate places." (Mark 1:45) The healed man's joy pushes the Healer back into the wilderness — the same wilderness where the whole chapter began. The Son of God ends where John started, on the outside, in the desolate places, because the crowd could not hold both the cure and the King, and chose the cure.

Paul would later write that God, "making his appeal through us," pleads, "be reconciled to God." (2 Corinthians 5:20) That is what has come near in the opening chapter of Mark. Not a program. Not a better, more spiritual version of the life you had already planned. A King who tears the sky open, wins the wilderness the first man lost, touches the untouchable with a hand that catches nothing and cleanses everything, and then walks past the crowd that only wanted the miracle — to preach in the next town, and the next, and the next, all the way to a hill where the sky tears a second time.

The kingdom has come near.

## The Authority They Could Not Forgive: Five Conflicts in Galilee (Mark 2:1-3:6)
*What happens when a man claims what only God may claim, and the guardians of God decide that authority this absolute has to die*

**Text:** Mark 2:1-3:6 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 43:25; Hosea 6:6; Exodus 20:8-11; Psalm 51:4; Daniel 7:13-14; Mark 12:10

The most dangerous thing Jesus does in these two chapters is not break a rule. Anyone can break a rule. The most dangerous thing he does is forgive — because forgiveness is a claim about who you are, and the men watching him understood the claim better than the crowd did. That is why they, and not the sinners, are the ones who walk out of these chapters plotting a murder.

We inherited a culture that has domesticated Jesus into a teacher of kindness, a rabbi of inclusion, a gentle man executed by the powerful for being too loving. Mark will not let that stand for two chapters. Mark tells you the religious professionals concluded he must be destroyed, and they concluded it not because he was soft but because he was making the specific claim that Yahweh alone had ever made in the history of Israel. You do not plot to kill a nice man. You plot to kill a man who forgives sins he was not sinned against, calls himself the bridegroom, and names himself Lord of the day God rested on.

### I. The Claim Under the Roof (Mark 2:1-12)

Four men tear open a roof and lower a paralytic through the hole they have made, and Jesus, seeing their faith, says the thing nobody in that house asked him to say: "Son, your sins are forgiven." (Mark 2:5) The man came for his legs. His friends carried him for his legs. Jesus goes for his guilt first, before anyone has said a word about it.

And the scribes reason in their hearts — Mark lets you overhear them think — "Why does this man speak like this? He is blaspheming. Who can forgive sins but God alone?" (Mark 2:7) And here is what has to be said plainly, because the whole scene turns on it: they were right. Right about the theology, wrong about the man in front of them. In Isaiah, Yahweh says, "I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake." (Isaiah 43:25) The first person, doubled, for emphasis — no one else does this. Only the offended party can forgive an offense. If you sin against your neighbor, I cannot absolve you; I was not the one wronged. David, who had sinned against Bathsheba and Uriah and a whole nation, still prayed, "Against you, you only, have I sinned." (Psalm 51:4) All sin is finally against God, which means only God can finally forgive it. So when a carpenter forgives a stranger's sins against God, he is either committing the highest blasphemy in the Torah or he is God himself standing in a crowded room in Capernaum. There is no third option, and the scribes knew it.

- **A. He heals the legs to prove the harder thing.** "Which is easier, to say... your sins are forgiven, or... rise, take up your bed and walk?" (Mark 2:9) Both are easy to *say*. Only one can be checked on the spot. Anyone can claim to forgive; no one can verify it. So the man walks in order that you will believe the invisible pardon on the strength of the visible cure. The miracle is evidence for the forgiveness. It is never the point in itself, and the moment a ministry makes the miracle the point, it has read this passage backward.
- **B. The scribes' logic is airtight and lands them on the wrong side of God.** This is the terror of the whole section. You can hold the doctrine of God perfectly, defend it zealously, and use it to condemn God to his face. Orthodoxy is not the same as allegiance. It never was. Getting God right on paper has never once guaranteed that you will recognize him when he walks into your synagogue.

### II. Mercy and Not Sacrifice: The Table, the Fast, the Sabbath (Mark 2:13-3:6)

Then it comes in a rush — five conflicts stacked like breaking waves, one after another. He calls Levi from the tax booth and eats in his house with tax collectors and sinners, and when the scribes ask why, he says, "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick... I came not to call the righteous, but sinners." (Mark 2:17) He hears Hosea underneath the whole quarrel: "For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice." (Hosea 6:6) Then they ask why his disciples do not fast, and he answers that the wedding guests do not fast while the bridegroom is with them — and he has just, in one breath, called himself the bridegroom, which is another name the Old Testament reserves for God alone, God the husband of an unfaithful Israel.

Then the Sabbath, twice, back to back. His disciples pluck heads of grain as they walk, and he answers that "the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath." (Mark 2:27-28) *Son of Man* is not a modest title; it is lifted from Daniel 7, where "one like a son of man" is given everlasting dominion and a kingdom that will not pass away. (Daniel 7:13-14) The Sabbath was God's own institution, rested into at creation, written by God's finger on stone at Sinai (Exodus 20:8-11) — and this man calls himself its Lord. Not its keeper. Its Lord.

- **A. Notice what the Pharisees were actually protecting.** They were not defending pleasure or wealth or power. They were defending the day God himself commanded them to keep holy. Their zeal was genuine. Steel-man them, because Mark's whole point collapses if you do not: they had watched Israel exiled to Babylon for covenant unfaithfulness, and they had built a hedge of rules around the law so that catastrophe would never happen to their people again. Their fence was, in its origin, an act of love for a wounded nation trying never to be wounded that way again. And it became the very thing they were willing to kill God to keep.
- **B. He heals the withered hand and asks the question they will not answer.** "Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill?" (Mark 3:4) They stay silent, because any honest answer indicts them. And Mark records that Jesus looked around at them "with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart." (Mark 3:5) Anger *and* grief, in a single clause. Not one or the other. He is furious at the hardness and heartbroken over the hard. That is the only anger the Scripture ever fully approves — the kind that grieves the very people it burns against. A prophet who is not also a pastor becomes a man who enjoys the indictment. Jesus never once does.

### III. When the Guardians Become the Executioners (Mark 3:6, and the mirror it holds up)

The chapter ends with a sentence that should make every lifelong religious person go cold. "The Pharisees went out and immediately held counsel with the Herodians against him, how to destroy him." (Mark 3:6) The Pharisees and the Herodians — the strict separatists who despised Rome and the political collaborators who profited from it, enemies who agreed on nothing under heaven — agree on this. And they agree by chapter three. Not at the cross. Not after some final, unbearable provocation near the end. This early, this fast, over a healed hand.

I have spent enough years inside the machinery of religion to know I am not reading about strangers. The men who first plotted his death were the ones who knew Scripture best, attended most faithfully, tithed most carefully, and cared most about getting God right. I am those men before I am ever the tax collector at the table. I have called my fear discernment. I have called my contempt conviction. I have defended the fence and slowly mistaken the fence for the field it was built to protect. The pattern in Mark 3 is not a first-century mistake made by unusually bad people. It is the standing temptation of everyone who loves the things of God enough to guard them — and then guards them against God himself when he finally arrives inconvenient, unclassifiable, and unwilling to submit to the hedge.

The church has done this in daylight, on the record, more than once. When the Reformation Europe of the 1520s and 30s met the Anabaptists — men and women who read the same Bible and reached different conclusions about the timing and mode of baptism — the guardians of right doctrine, Protestant and Catholic alike, drowned them in the rivers, a grim parody of the very sacrament they were fighting over. Zealous men, defending truth they genuinely held, killing to keep it clean. The hand that grips a doctrine hardest is the hand most easily closed into a fist. Mark 3:6 is not safely behind us in the first century. It stands at the front of every generation that decides its correctness has licensed its cruelty.

- **A. The two hungers finally separate here.** The sick came to be healed; the healthy came to be proven right. And it was the healthy, the qualified, the correct who could not forgive the authority that exposed them. Grace offends the righteous far more than it offends the guilty, because grace tells the righteous their standing was never earned in the first place.
- **B. The rejected One becomes the cornerstone.** Jesus will later quote it against these very men: "The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone." (Mark 12:10) The builders — the professionals, the experts, the ones whose whole job was to know which stone belonged in the wall — threw out the only stone that would hold the building up. Mark is telling you at chapter three exactly how chapter fifteen ends, and daring you, the faithful reader who has come to church your whole life, to ask which builder you are.

They plotted to destroy him.

## Naming the True Family: The Unforgivable Sin and the New Kinship (Mark 3:7-35)
*Two verdicts collide over one man — that he is possessed, and that he is insane — and Jesus answers by redrawing the boundaries of blood*

**Text:** Mark 3:7-35 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 49:24-25; Genesis 3:15; Hebrews 2:11-12; 1 John 3:8; Matthew 7:21; Deuteronomy 33:9

There is a particular loneliness reserved for the person whose own family thinks he has lost his mind and whose religious community thinks he is in league with hell. Mark puts both charges in one chapter, side by side, framing the appointment of the Twelve. It is a deliberate sandwich, one of Mark's signature moves: the family comes out to seize him, the scribes come down to accuse him, then the family reappears at the door. He wraps the single worst accusation ever made against Jesus inside the people who should have been the first to defend him.

Our age has made *family* the last sacred word. When every other loyalty dissolved — church, nation, neighborhood, vocation — blood was supposed to remain, the one bond you did not choose and could not lose. And Jesus, of all people, is the one who stands in a crowded house and relativizes it in front of everyone — not to abolish family, and not out of coldness, but to found a deeper one, and to warn that being close to him by birth or by proximity or by long attendance saves no one at all.

### I. The Twelve Appointed, the Crowd Pressing (Mark 3:7-19)

The crowds come from everywhere — Galilee, Judea, Jerusalem, Idumea, beyond the Jordan, from around Tyre and Sidon — until Jesus has to keep a boat ready so he is not physically crushed against the shore. And out of that ocean of need, that sea of people who want something from him, he does something small and strange and strategic: he goes up on a mountain and appoints twelve men. Twelve, for the twelve tribes of Israel. He is not merely recruiting helpers to handle the volume. He is refounding Israel from a mountain, the way it was founded at Sinai, and the number is the entire argument in a single digit.

He appoints them, Mark says, for two things: "that they might be with him and he might send them out to preach." (Mark 3:14) *With him* first. *Sent* second. The order is not incidental, and it is not reversible. Everything the modern leader gets wrong about ministry is compressed in flipping those two clauses — becoming a sending without a with, a function without a presence, a mouth without a life behind it. He builds men before he deploys them, and he builds them by keeping them near.

- **A. He chooses the Twelve while the crowd waits below.** The multitude is real and pressing and desperate, and he deliberately turns from it to invest in a handful of ordinary men. Depth in a few over spectacle for the many. The kingdom advances the way it was always going to advance: slowly, relationally, through people who had first been *with him* long enough to be changed by the nearness.
- **B. Judas is named in the list.** "and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him." (Mark 3:19) Mark cannot even finish the roll call without the shadow already inside it. The betrayer is not a later intruder who slipped past the vetting. He is an insider from the first naming. Proximity is not the same as loyalty — the very theme of the whole chapter, planted quietly here in the last name on the list.

### II. A House Divided: The Charge and the Blasphemy (Mark 3:20-30)

The scribes come down from Jerusalem — the officials, sent from the center of power to evaluate this Galilean disturbance — and they arrive with an explanation for his undeniable power over demons: "He is possessed by Beelzebul, and by the prince of demons he casts out the demons." (Mark 3:22) They cannot deny the exorcisms; the works are too public and too many. So they attribute them to hell. The rescue is real, so they call the rescuer a devil.

And Jesus answers with plain, patient logic. "How can Satan cast out Satan? If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand." (Mark 3:24) A house at war with itself falls. Satan does not evict Satan; a devil does not war against his own dominion. Then the real claim, the one the whole exchange was building toward: "No one can enter a strong man's house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man. Then indeed he may plunder his house." (Mark 3:27) Isaiah had asked the impossible question — "Can the prey be taken from the mighty, or the captives of a tyrant be rescued?" — and answered that yes, even the captives of the tyrant would be freed. (Isaiah 49:24-25) Jesus is the one who has walked into the strong man's house, the domain Satan has ruled since Eden, since the serpent was told a woman's seed would crush his head (Genesis 3:15), and he is carrying the furniture out the front door in broad daylight. Every exorcism in Mark is a burglary. The kingdom of God, seen from below, looks like a robbery in progress. That is exactly what John means when he writes that "the reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil." (1 John 3:8)

- **A. The unforgivable sin is not a slip of the tongue.** "Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness, but is guilty of an eternal sin." (Mark 3:29) People have tortured themselves over this verse for centuries, lying awake certain they have crossed a line. Read it in its context. The scribes are looking directly at undeniable liberation — a man freed, the finger of God visibly rescuing the oppressed — and calling it demonic. To stare at the Spirit's rescue and name it hell, and to keep naming it that with your eyes open, is to slam shut the only door mercy ever comes through. The sin is not that you once cursed in a dark hour. It is that you have looked at the light, decided it is darkness, and settled there permanently.
- **B. The person terrified of having committed it almost certainly has not.** The scribes were not afraid. They were smug. They had a category ready and slotted God into it without a tremor. A conscience that fears grieving God is a conscience the Spirit is still actively working. The hard heart, the truly blasphemed-against-the-Spirit heart, does not lie awake worrying. It sleeps fine. That is the whole horror of the condition, and the strange comfort for the one afraid of it.

### III. Whoever Does the Will of God (Mark 3:31-35)

His mother and his brothers arrive — the same family that back in verse 21 had said "he is out of his mind" and gone out to seize him and take him home by force. Now they stand outside the house and send word in, calling for him. And Jesus, sitting inside with the crowd seated in a circle around him, asks, "Who are my mother and my brothers?" and looking around at those seated with him, says, "Here are my mother and my brothers. Whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother." (Mark 3:34-35)

I want to be careful here, because this is precisely the kind of verse a man twists to justify neglecting the people in his own house. Jesus is not despising Mary; he will provide for her tenderly from the cross itself, handing her to the beloved disciple. He is doing something more unsettling than dismissing his family. He is founding one. He is saying that the deepest kinship in the universe is not carried in blood but in obedience — and that a stranger doing the Father's will is nearer to him than a brother by birth who is not. He says it flatly elsewhere: "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father." (Matthew 7:21) Moses had blessed the tribe of Levi long before for saying of their own kin, "I regard them not" when the covenant was at stake. (Deuteronomy 33:9) The claim of God cuts across the claim of blood.

I have to sit down inside that, because I have traded on proximity my whole life. I grew up fatherless, and when I found the church I found fathers and brothers I was not born to — and I have also, quietly, in seasons I am not proud of, assumed that my position near the center of Christian things counted as being in the family. It does not. The scribes were near. His own family was nearest of all, and standing outside the door, calling for a man they had come to collect. Nearness to Jesus has never once been the same thing as belonging to him. You can be in the room, on the payroll, in the pulpit, and outside the family.

The early church understood this in a way that got it killed. In the second and third centuries, Roman society was organized entirely by blood, household, and civic religion; to be a Christian was to be accused, by Tacitus and others, of *odium generis humani* — hatred of the human race — precisely because these people called slaves and masters brothers at the same table, buried the strangers' dead as their own, and treated a fellow believer they had never met as closer than kin. Around the year 197, Tertullian records the astonishment of the pagans watching them: "See how they love one another." They had learned it in a crowded house in Galilee, from a man who looked around a circle of nobodies and called them mother and brother. The writer of Hebrews says this is exactly why Jesus "is not ashamed to call them brothers." (Hebrews 2:11) The Son who was called insane by his own founds a family for everyone else who was ever left standing outside.

- **A. The will of God, not the accident of birth, is the door.** You cannot be born into this family. There is no bloodline, no inheritance, no last name that admits you. You can only be adopted, and the adoption runs through obedience, and the obedience runs through faith in the One who is even now binding the strong man and emptying his house.
- **B. The rejected Son becomes the elder brother of the rejected.** The man his own family called mad opens his family to everyone the world has called nothing. That is not sentiment, and it is not a warm closing thought. It is the strong man's house being emptied of its prisoners, one adopted child at a time, and every adoption is a fresh burglary against the tyrant.

Doing God's will makes family.

## Even Wind and Sea Obey: The Word Sown and the Storm Stilled (Mark 4:1-41)
*Why the same word produces such different soil, why the kingdom grows hidden and small, and why the men in the boat had to ask who this is*

**Text:** Mark 4:1-41 · **Supporting:** Psalm 107:28-29; Isaiah 6:9-10; Psalm 65:7; Job 38:8-11; Jonah 1:15; Daniel 7:2-3

Mark 4 is built to make you ask one question, and it deliberately withholds the answer until the last verse. The chapter opens in a boat, teaching a crowd on the shore, and it closes in the same boat, the men terrified, and between the two the disciples move from studying the kingdom to being nearly swallowed by it. The parables were preparing them for the storm the whole time. They just did not know the sea was going to be part of the lesson.

We are the soil the parable warns about most. Not the hard path, not the shallow rocky ground — the thorns. Ours is a culture engineered, at industrial scale, to grow thorns: the cares of the world, the deceitfulness of riches, and the desire for other things, all of it delivered on demand into the palm of your hand a thousand times a day. The word gets in. Then the thorns get in after it, and Jesus tells you exactly what they do. They do not pull the plant up by the roots. They choke it, slowly, quietly, until it is alive and fruitless and can no longer tell the difference between the two.

### I. The Sower and the Soils (Mark 4:1-20)

A sower went out to sow. Some seed fell along the path and the birds came and ate it. Some fell on rocky ground where it had little soil, and it sprang up fast and withered faster, having no root. Some fell among thorns and the thorns grew up and choked it, and it yielded nothing. And some fell into good soil and produced grain, growing up and increasing and yielding thirtyfold, sixtyfold, a hundredfold. (Mark 4:3-8)

Notice what the parable is not about. It is not about the sower's technique, his aim, or the quality of the seed — the seed is identical in every case, scattered by the same hand. The only variable in the entire parable is the ground it lands on. The same word, preached to the same crowd, in the same hour, by the same voice, lands in four kinds of heart and does four completely different things. This is the honest answer to a question every preacher and every praying parent secretly asks in the dark: why does the same gospel save one child and slide clean off another raised at the same table? Jesus does not soften it or dodge it. The word is not the variable. The heart is.

- **A. The rocky soil is the most frightening, precisely because it looks exactly like the good soil at first.** It springs up "immediately." (Mark 4:5) In week one, the enthusiastic convert and the genuinely transformed one are indistinguishable — same tears, same volume, same visible joy. The difference is root, and root is invisible, and root is only ever tested by heat. "When tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately they fall away." (Mark 4:17) The test of soil is never the sunshine. It is always the drought.
- **B. Fruit is the only category Jesus finally uses to measure the real.** Not sprouting speed, not emotional intensity, not how loud it came up. Fruit — thirty, sixty, a hundredfold. He is remarkably patient with the *amount* and utterly ruthless about its *existence*. A plant that never bears anything was never good soil, however green and promising it looked in April. That should sober every one of us who has mistaken a strong start for a saved soul, our own included.

### II. The Kingdom That Grows in the Dark (Mark 4:21-34)

Then two seed parables that answer the disciples' quiet, unspoken disappointment. If Jesus is truly the King, then where is the kingdom? It looks so small. It looks like a Galilean and twelve fishermen and a crowd that mostly wants lunch. And he tells them: the kingdom is like a man who scatters seed on the ground, and "he sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how." (Mark 4:27) The earth produces by itself — the Greek word is *automatē*, from which we get *automatic*. The farmer does not manufacture the growth. He cannot even explain it. He plants, and he sleeps, and the kingdom comes up out of the dark ground without him and without his understanding.

And it is like a mustard seed, "the smallest of all the seeds on earth," that becomes the largest of the garden plants and puts out large branches, so the birds nest in its shade. (Mark 4:31-32) The kingdom does not arrive the way empires arrive, with legions and proclamations and the sound of marching. It arrives small, hidden, easy to overlook, easy to despise — and then it is everywhere at once, and no one can point to the day it happened.

- **A. This is a direct rebuke to every leader who thinks the growth depends on him.** I have lain awake strategizing the harvest as though the germinating were my responsibility, as though the kingdom would stall if I stopped managing it. And Jesus says the man sleeps and rises and the seed grows and he knows not how. The most freeing sentence a pastor can ever hear is that he cannot make one single seed germinate by force of will or strategy. Plant, sleep, and let God give the increase. The sleeping is not negligence. In this parable, the sleeping is faith.
- **B. Smallness is not failure; it is the chosen method.** A generation raised on metrics and dashboards reads "smallest of all seeds" as a problem to be fixed. Jesus reads it as the design. The kingdom's disguise is its size. It looks like nothing worth watching until the birds are nesting in its branches, and by then no empire on earth can uproot it.

### III. Who Then Is This? (Mark 4:35-41)

Evening comes. "Let us go across to the other side." (Mark 4:35) And a great windstorm rises on the lake, sudden the way that lake is known to do, the waves breaking into the boat until it is filling with water — and Jesus is asleep on a cushion in the stern. The men who fish this water for a living, who know a killing storm from a scare, who have buried friends in this lake, are certain they are about to die, and their teacher is asleep. They wake him with an accusation dressed as a question: "Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?" (Mark 4:38)

He wakes, and he rebukes the wind, and he says to the sea, "Peace! Be still." (Mark 4:39) The Greek is *siōpa, pephimōso* — literally, "be silent, be muzzled" — the very same word he uses to silence a demon in chapter one. He speaks to the storm the way he speaks to hell, as to a hostile power under his command, and the wind drops instantly, and there is a great calm on the water. Then he turns to the men in the boat: "Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith?" (Mark 4:40)

And here is the sentence the entire chapter was engineered to produce. "And they were filled with great fear, and said to one another, 'Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?'" (Mark 4:41) A moment ago they were afraid of the storm. Now they are more afraid of the man who stopped it. Because every Jew in that boat knew the Scriptures, and the Scriptures said only one Person commands the raging sea. "You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them." (Psalm 65:7) It was God who "shut in the sea with doors" and said, "Thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed." (Job 38:8-11) The psalmist sang of terrified sailors in a tempest that when they cried out, "he made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed." (Psalm 107:29) In Daniel's vision the churning sea is the source of every beast and empire that ever terrorized the earth. (Daniel 7:2-3) The sea, in the Hebrew imagination, is chaos itself, the thing only God has ever mastered. And it is asleep on a cushion in their boat.

I have to tell you exactly where I usually stand in this story, because it is not with the calm and confident. I am the one shaking a sleeping God and demanding to know if he cares. And notice the thing that is easy to miss: he never once answers the question they actually asked. They asked, "Do you not care," and he never says, "Of course I care." He answers a deeper question they did not know they were asking — not *do you care* but *who am I*. Because the fear underneath "do you not care" is really "are you enough," and the storm was the only classroom in the world that could teach it. He let them into the boat, and he let the storm come, and he slept — not because he did not care, but because the lesson was who he is, and you cannot learn that lesson in calm water. Faith is not built in the harbor.

The church has known this from the beginning, and staked everything on it. When Athanasius stood almost entirely alone against the whole imperial-backed Arian consensus of the fourth century — *Athanasius contra mundum*, Athanasius against the world, driven into exile five separate times between 335 and 366 — the thing he refused to surrender was that the man asleep in the boat was fully God, of one substance with the Father, not a lesser created being. Everything hung on it, and he knew it. If the one who muzzled the sea was merely a great teacher, then the boat is empty of God and the storm wins in the end. The whole Nicene fight of 325 was, when you strip it down, a fight over the identity of the man the disciples were afraid of. Get him wrong, make him one degree less than God, and there is no great calm coming — only the wind, and the water rising, and no one in the stern who can stop it.

- **A. The presence of Christ is not the absence of the storm.** He was in the boat, and the storm came anyway. Faith is not the boat that never floods and the life that never floods. It is the settled certainty that the One asleep in the stern commands the very thing that is flooding it, and will speak to it when it is time.
- **B. The question is still the only question worth answering.** "Who then is this?" Every other question the Gospel raises bends back to this one and waits on it. Answer it, and the storm changes meaning entirely. Refuse it, keep it academic, and no calm the world can offer will ever be calm enough.

Even wind and sea obey.

## Do Not Fear, Only Believe: Authority Over What We Cannot Touch (Mark 5:1-43)
*A man no chains could hold, a woman twelve years unclean, and a girl already mourned as dead — three walls, one hand, and a power that catches nothing and cleanses everything*

**Text:** Mark 5:1-43 · **Supporting:** Leviticus 15:25-27; Numbers 19:11; Isaiah 65:4; Psalm 30:11; Hosea 13:14; 1 Corinthians 15:26

Mark 4 ended with a question — who then is this? — and Mark 5 answers it three separate times, in three places no first-century Jew would willingly set foot: a Gentile graveyard overrun with pigs, the shame of a bleeding woman in a crowd, and a house already full of professional mourners. Jesus walks straight into the three great uncleannesses of that world — the demonic, the defiled, and the dead — and comes out of each one carrying life, and touching nothing that touches him back.

We have our own untouchables. We did not abolish the category; we just moved it and renamed it. We no longer fear ceremonial defilement, but we fear the people whose brokenness might rub off on us — the addict, the ex-con, the one whose grief has dragged on so long it has become uncomfortable to sit near, the shame we would much rather manage from a safe and Christian distance. Mark 5 is a chapter about what Jesus does with exactly the people we have quietly agreed cannot be helped and should not be touched. He does not help them from across the room. He goes to the tombs.

### I. The Man No Chains Could Hold (Mark 5:1-20)

They cross to the country of the Gerasenes, Gentile territory, unclean ground, and the moment Jesus steps out of the boat a man with an unclean spirit comes out of the tombs to meet him — a man who "lived among the tombs. And no one could bind him anymore, not even with a chain." (Mark 5:3) They had tried. Night and day he tore the shackles apart and broke the irons on his feet, and he was there among the graves, "crying out and cutting himself with stones." (Mark 5:5) Isaiah had described the people in open rebellion against God as those "who sit in tombs, and spend the night in secret places." (Isaiah 65:4) This man is every category of unclean at once — Gentile, demon-possessed, self-lacerating, living among corpses. He is the farthest gone that a Jewish reader could possibly imagine, the human being everyone had written off, chained, and finally abandoned to the graveyard.

And he runs to Jesus. The demons name themselves — "My name is Legion, for we are many" (Mark 5:9) — a Roman military term, some six thousand soldiers to a legion, an occupying army lodged inside one man. They beg not to be sent out of the country, and Jesus permits them to enter a herd of pigs, and the two thousand swine rush down the bank and drown themselves in the sea. The town comes out to see, and they find the man they had chained and feared "sitting there, clothed and in his right mind." (Mark 5:15) And here is the sentence that should stop you cold: "and they were afraid." Not grateful. Not amazed and glad. Afraid. And they begin to beg Jesus to leave their region.

- **A. The town preferred the demoniac to the deliverer.** They had long ago made their peace with the screaming man in the tombs. He was a known cost, budgeted for, contained. They had never for one moment made peace with a power that could cost them two thousand pigs in an afternoon and undo the arrangement they had settled into. A community will tolerate a familiar horror over an unfamiliar holiness every single time, because the horror it can price and manage, and the holiness it cannot control.
- **B. The healed man wants to follow, and is told instead to stay.** He begs to get in the boat and go with Jesus, the most understandable request in the chapter. Jesus says no — "Go home to your friends and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you." (Mark 5:19) The first missionary Jesus sends into the Gentile Decapolis is a man who, one hour earlier, was cutting himself among the graves. Your worst chapter, the one you would pay any amount to erase, is exactly the testimony he sends back into the town that once feared you.

### II. The Woman and the Girl: Two Twelves and One Touch (Mark 5:21-43)

Back across the sea, in the press of another crowd, a ruler of the synagogue named Jairus falls at his feet — a man of standing, on his knees in the dirt in public, because his little daughter is dying. And on the way to Jairus's house, the crowd pressing in on all sides, a woman "who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years" (Mark 5:25) comes up behind Jesus in the crush and touches his garment. Twelve years. Under the law of Leviticus 15, her condition made her permanently, chronically unclean, and everything she sat on unclean, and everyone she touched unclean. (Leviticus 15:25-27) For twelve years she has been shut out of the temple worship, unable to be embraced without contaminating whoever held her, a leper without the leprosy. She has spent everything she had on physicians and only grown worse under their care. And she thinks to herself, "If I touch even his garments, I will be made well." (Mark 5:28)

By every rule she has ever known, her touch should defile him. That is the only direction uncleanness ever flows in that world — outward, always outward, always contaminating the clean. She reaches out in the crowd expecting, at most, to steal a cure and slip away unnoticed in the shame she has carried for over a decade. And the current runs backward. Her touch does not defile him; his purity heals her. "Immediately the flow of blood dried up, and she felt in her body that she was healed of her disease." (Mark 5:29) The one thing that could never be touched has just touched the Holy One of God, and instead of catching her uncleanness, he has cured it in an instant.

Then Jesus does the thing that changes the whole scene from a healing into a homecoming: he stops. In a crowd, on the way to a dying child, with a frantic father beside him counting the minutes, he stops to ask, "Who touched my garments?" (Mark 5:30) Not because he does not know. Because *she* needs him to. He will not let her leave with a stolen healing and her shame still intact. He draws her out, and she comes trembling, and she falls down before him and tells him the whole truth, and he says the word she has not heard in twelve years: "Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace, and be healed of your disease." (Mark 5:34) *Daughter.* Twelve years untouchable, unnamed, an embarrassment in the crowd — and the first word he gives her is the word for belonging.

- **A. He healed the woman's body instantly and her shame deliberately.** The cure was silent and secret; he made it public and personal on purpose, at the cost of precious time. He would not let her walk away carrying a healed body and a hidden shame. Grace that heals the symptom and leaves the shame to fester is not the grace Jesus gives anyone in this Gospel.
- **B. And while he tarries for her, the child dies.** Word comes up the road: "Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further?" (Mark 5:35) The delay for the bleeding woman has cost Jairus his window, and every parent reading this feels the injustice of it in their chest. And Jesus, overhearing the message, ignoring it, says to Jairus the sentence that holds the whole chapter together in six words: "Do not fear, only believe." (Mark 5:36)

### III. Talitha Cumi, and the Enemy That Is Not Final (Mark 5:37-43)

He comes to the house, and the mourning is already in full swing — the professional wailers hired for the occasion, the flutes, the tumult and commotion of a first-century funeral already underway before the body is cold. He walks in and says, "The child is not dead but sleeping," and they laugh at him. (Mark 5:39) They laugh, because they are professionals and they know death when they see it, and they are entirely right that she is dead, and entirely wrong that it is final. He puts them all outside — the mockery has no place in the room where he is about to work — and takes only the father and mother and the three disciples, and he takes the dead child by the hand.

Touch a corpse under the law of Numbers 19 and you are unclean for seven days. (Numbers 19:11) Every person in that house knows it in their bones. He takes her hand anyway. And Mark, who almost never gives us the original Aramaic, gives us the exact words this one time, the way you remember the exact words of the moment that undid you: "Talitha cumi," which means, "Little girl, I say to you, arise." (Mark 5:41) And immediately she gets up and begins to walk, and they are overcome with amazement. And then comes the most tender detail in the whole Gospel — he tells them "to give her something to eat." (Mark 5:43) The Lord of life who has just walked into a corpse's room and conquered the grave notices, in the same breath, that the little girl is hungry.

I have stood in that house. I have done funerals for children, and I have sat with parents in the corridor where the news comes down the hall, and I will not stand here and pretend to you that "do not fear, only believe" is an easy word to say in that room. It is not a slogan, and anyone who has used it as one has not been in the corridor. It is a command, and it only means anything at all if the man who gives it can do what he did in Jairus's house. Take the resurrection away and it becomes cruelty — telling a grieving parent not to fear the thing that has already happened to their child. Leave the resurrection in, and it is suddenly the only word strong enough to be spoken into that corridor at all. And here is the sober honesty of it: the girl he raised in Mark 5 died again, later, an old woman. He was not sparing her from death forever. He was showing her, and Jairus, and every reader since, who holds the keys to the one room we are all most afraid of.

The early church staked its entire existence on this, and it changed how they died and how they buried. In the plagues that swept the Roman empire — the Antonine plague beginning around 165, the plague of Cyprian around 249 — Christians buried their dead facing east and called the burial ground a *koimētērion*, a *cemetery*, a word that simply means a sleeping-place, a dormitory. They took the very word Jesus spoke over the girl — she is not dead but sleeping — and carved it into stone over the bones of their own children. A pagan buried a body and was finished. A Christian put someone to bed. The sociologist Rodney Stark has argued that this refusal to fear death was a large part of why the church grew steadily while the empire died around it — believers who nursed the sick and did not flee, because they had heard *talitha cumi* and knew what the last enemy actually was. Paul names it: "The last enemy to be destroyed is death." (1 Corinthians 15:26) An enemy — real, hated, never to be sentimentalized or called a friend. But the last one. And already, in a small house in Galilee, disarmed by a hand that should have been defiled and instead gave a dead girl her supper.

- **A. The demonic, the defiled, and the dead all yield to the same hand.** Three walls we cannot get past on our own — the evil we cannot cast out, the shame we cannot wash off, the death we cannot reverse — and one man walks straight through all three in a single chapter and comes out the other side clean and carrying life. He is either that, exactly that, or he is nothing worth the giving of your Sunday.
- **B. "Do not fear, only believe" is a command, not a comfort.** He does not say *do not grieve*; grief is honest and he weeps himself. He says *do not let fear have the last word*, because he is about to have it instead. The command is only bearable, only sane, because the tomb is empty three chapters from the end of the book, and death has already had its taunt thrown back in its face: "O death, where are your plagues? O Sheol, where is your sting?" (Hosea 13:14)

Do not fear, only believe.

## You Are the Christ: Who Do You Say I Am (Mark 6:30-44; 8:1-30)
*Twice he feeds thousands from almost nothing, twice they miss what the bread reveals, and at Caesarea Philippi the whole book turns on one man's answer*

**Text:** Mark 6:30-44; 8:1-30 · **Supporting:** Psalm 23:1-2; Exodus 16:4; Ezekiel 34:5,23; Isaiah 40:11; Daniel 7:13-14; 2 Corinthians 4:4

Mark 8 sits at the exact structural center of the Gospel, and Mark built it that way on purpose. Everything before it climbs toward one question, and everything after it descends toward one hill outside Jerusalem. The hinge is a conversation on a road in the far north, near Caesarea Philippi, where Jesus asks his disciples the only question the whole book has been asking, and Peter finally answers it out loud — and then immediately proves he has no idea what his own right answer means.

We live downstream of a great deal of confident opinion about Jesus. He has been claimed by every side of every fight, remade into a life coach, a social revolutionary, a moral teacher, a mascot, a symbol of whatever the age had already decided it wanted. The crowds in Mark 8 had their opinions too — John the Baptist raised, Elijah returned, one of the prophets — and every one of them was respectful, and every single one of them was wrong. Getting Jesus wrong almost never feels like getting him wrong from the inside. It usually feels like getting him admirably, respectfully, almost right.

### I. Twice the Bread, Twice the Blindness (Mark 6:30-44; 8:1-10)

The disciples come back from their preaching mission exhausted, and Jesus takes them away to a desolate place to rest, and the crowd runs ahead on foot and finds them there — five thousand men, besides women and children. And Mark tells you the thing that governs the entire scene: "he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd." (Mark 6:34) That phrase is not a soft, pastoral sentiment. It is lifted straight out of Ezekiel 34, where God indicts the false shepherds of Israel who fed only themselves and let the flock be scattered and become food for every wild beast (Ezekiel 34:5), and then promises, "I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David, and he shall feed them." (Ezekiel 34:23) When Jesus looks at that crowd and sees sheep without a shepherd, he is quietly identifying himself as the promised Shepherd-King. And what does the true Shepherd do the moment he sees them? He commands them to sit down "on the green grass" (Mark 6:39) — the green pastures of Psalm 23, "he makes me lie down in green pastures" — and he feeds them bread in the wilderness, exactly the way God fed Israel with bread from heaven in Exodus 16. Bread, in the desert, from heaven, through the Shepherd who is also the King who is also, it turns out, God. The whole Old Testament is folded into this one meal on the grass.

Then he does the entire thing again — four thousand this time, in chapter 8, in similarly desolate country. And in between the two feedings, the disciples are in a boat fretting because they forgot to bring bread, and Jesus, grieved, says to them, "Do you not yet perceive or understand? Are your hearts hardened? Having eyes do you not see, and having ears do you not hear?... How many baskets full of broken pieces did you take up?" (Mark 8:17-19) They can recite the numbers back to him — twelve baskets after the first, seven after the second — and still completely miss what the baskets are for. The bread was never mainly about hunger. It was a sign pointing at the identity of the one breaking it. And they counted the leftovers with precision and missed the Shepherd standing in front of them.

- **A. The disciples had the miracle memorized and the meaning hidden.** They could give you the exact statistics of both feedings and still panic over one forgotten loaf in the bottom of the boat. It is entirely possible to have the facts of the gospel by heart, chapter and verse, and remain, in the way that finally counts, blind. That is not the crowd's condition Mark is worried about. It is the condition of the insiders, the ones nearest to Jesus, and it should worry every one of us who has memorized more than we have seen.
- **B. Jesus provides in the wilderness the way only God provides.** Two feedings, both in desolate places, both echoing the manna of the exodus, both leaving baskets left over — abundance, not mere sufficiency. God does not feed his people to the edge and stop; he feeds them until there is more than they can carry. The sign is stacked and repeated twice because the thing it points to is the single hardest thing in the whole book to actually see.

### II. The Blind Man and the Confession (Mark 8:22-30)

Then Mark does something that no accident of arrangement could produce. Right before the great confession at Caesarea Philippi, he places a healing found in no other Gospel — and it is the only miracle in all four Gospels that Jesus performs in two distinct stages. A blind man at Bethsaida is brought to him. Jesus spits on the man's eyes, lays hands on him, and asks what he sees, and the man says, "I see men, but they look like trees, walking." (Mark 8:24) Partial sight. Real sight, genuine, and not yet clear. Then Jesus lays his hands on the man's eyes a second time, and he looks intently, and his sight is restored, and he sees everything clearly. (Mark 8:25)

Mark put that two-stage healing exactly there on purpose. Because the very next scene is a man who is about to see partially — to see something completely true and not yet see it clearly at all. This is Mark's structural genius, and it is easy to walk past. The two-stage healing is a living parable of Peter, laid down in the text one paragraph before Peter is going to need it.

- **A. Partial sight of Jesus is still, in the end, blindness.** "Men like trees walking" is not sight; it is a shape without a truth, a form without a face. A Jesus you have half-right — the teacher without the cross, the healer without the throne, the miracle-worker without the suffering — is exactly the man like a tree, walking. It looks like seeing. It sounds like a confession. It is not yet seeing.
- **B. The second touch is the mercy.** Jesus does not scold the half-blind man for seeing poorly. He does not send him away half-healed as a lesson. He simply touches him again. The partial seer is not rejected; he is finished, completed, brought all the way through. And that is grace to every one of us whose sight of Christ is still coming clear, which is all of us on our very best day. He does not abandon the half-seeing. He touches them again.

### III. The Christ Who Must Suffer, and the Cross We Would Rather Rewrite (Mark 8:27-30)

On the road to the villages of Caesarea Philippi — a city Herod's son had built and named for Caesar, crowned with a gleaming temple to the divine Augustus, sitting at the foot of a great cliff riddled with pagan shrines to the god Pan — Jesus asks his disciples, "Who do people say that I am?" And they report back the crowd's respectful, admiring, wrong answers. Then he turns the whole thing on them: "But who do you say that I am?" And Peter answers, "You are the Christ." (Mark 8:29) There it is at last. The confession the entire book has been climbing toward for eight chapters. The right answer, finally spoken out loud, in the shadow of Caesar's temple, in the one place on earth where the raw political stakes of the word *Christ* — the anointed King, the one Daniel saw given everlasting dominion (Daniel 7:13-14) — could not possibly be louder or more dangerous.

And then — this is the part we skip, the part the felt-board leaves out — Jesus "began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and the chief priests and the scribes and be killed, and after three days rise again." (Mark 8:31) And Peter, who thirty seconds ago got the title exactly right, takes him aside and begins to rebuke him for it. The man who just confessed the Christ cannot tolerate for one moment what the Christ has actually come to do. And Jesus turns, and looking at his disciples, says the hardest words he ever spoke to a friend: "Get behind me, Satan. For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man." (Mark 8:33) The same word — Satan — he threw at the tempter in the wilderness. For one sentence Peter has become the very voice of the wilderness temptation: take the crown, skip the cross, have the kingdom without the dying.

Here is where I have to stop preaching down at Peter and come stand beside him in the dirt of that road. Because I want the Christ without the suffering too. I want a Jesus who fixes my circumstances, funds my plans, blesses my nation, guards my comfort, and validates the life I had already decided to live before I met him — and who asks me to carry no cross at all. I have preached, in weak and tired seasons I am not proud of, a Christ who is mostly a means to the ends I already wanted, and that is precisely, exactly, Peter's sin at Caesarea Philippi. Right title. Wrong king. The name confessed with the whole mouth and the cross quietly cut out. It is entirely possible to say the words "You are the Christ" and mean by them a messiah who exists to save me the trouble of dying to myself. That is not seeing clearly. That is a man like a tree, walking, one paragraph after Bethsaida, still needing the second touch.

The church has fought this exact battle in the full daylight of history, and it cost lives. In the 1930s, when the German Christian movement bent the gospel around the *Führer* and quietly reduced Jesus to the guarantor of a national and racial destiny, it was a handful of pastors and theologians who gathered at Barmen in May of 1934 and confessed, against the entire current of their own culture, that "Jesus Christ, as he is attested for us in Holy Scripture, is the one Word of God whom we have to hear and whom we have to trust and obey in life and in death." They were saying, at real and terrible cost — Bonhoeffer would hang for it at Flossenbürg in April of 1945, Niemöller would spend years in the camps — that you cannot keep the name of Christ while handing his throne to Caesar. That is the Caesarea Philippi test, and every generation faces it standing in the shadow of its own temple to its own emperor, whatever the emperor is called this century. The right confession and the wrong king is not a first-century problem safely behind us. Paul warned that "the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers." (2 Corinthians 4:4) But the blinding is not always unbelief. Sometimes it is a full-throated confession with the cross carefully cut out of the middle of it.

- **A. The confession is only true if the cross is inside it.** "You are the Christ" is the right answer and an empty one, a hollow shell, until you let the Christ himself define what the word means — a King who reigns from a cross, not around it, not over it, not after skipping it. Peter had the noun exactly right and lost the meaning of it in the very same breath, and so can we.
- **B. To follow the Christ you confess, take up the cross you would rather rewrite.** Immediately after rebuking Peter, Jesus calls the crowd and says, "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me." (Mark 8:34) The confession that costs nothing saves no one. The Christ you can carry in your pocket without dying to a single thing is a Christ you have manufactured yourself — a shape, a form, a tree, walking. The real one asks first for the second touch to see him clearly, and then, having been seen, he asks for your life.

You are the Christ.

## Glory on the Mountain, Greatness in the Valley: Mark 9:1-50
*What the Father says on the summit, the Son works out in the dust*

**Text:** Mark 9:1-50 · **Supporting:** Exodus 24:15-18; 2 Peter 1:16-18; Philippians 2:5-8; Isaiah 66:24; Matthew 18:1-4

We want the mountain without the valley. We want the light on the face and the voice from the cloud, the moment of clarity that settles everything, and then we want to build a shelter and stay. Peter wanted that. Six days after Jesus told him the Son of Man must suffer and be killed, Peter climbed a mountain, saw the glory, and immediately tried to move in. And the Father interrupted him mid-sentence. Because the mountain is not the point. The mountain is what makes the valley bearable, and the valley is where the Son of God is going.

This chapter is one of the most honest passages in the New Testament, because it puts the summit and the valley on the same page and refuses to let us keep them apart. Nine verses of blinding glory. Forty verses of failure, argument, and a warning about hell. Mark will not let us have the transfiguration without the demon-possessed boy, or the Father's voice without the disciples fighting over rank on the road to a cross. He knows the temptation of every religious person, and he refuses to feed it. The temptation is to collect mountaintop moments and skip the discipleship. Jesus came down the mountain. That is the sermon before the sermon.

### I. The Voice from the Cloud: Listen to Him (Mark 9:1-13)

Mark ties the transfiguration to the confession before it with a chain of time — "after six days" — the only such marker in a Gospel that usually moves with the word "immediately." Something is being finished here. Peter had confessed Jesus as the Christ at Caesarea Philippi. Then Jesus said the Christ must suffer, and Peter rebuked him, and Jesus called Peter Satan. The confession was right and the imagination behind it was pagan. So the Father takes three men up a high mountain to correct the imagination.

"And he was transfigured before them, and his clothes became radiant, intensely white, as no one on earth could bleach them. And there appeared to them Elijah with Moses, and they were talking with Jesus." (Mark 9:2-4) The Greek is *metemorphōthē* — the form itself changed, the glory that was always there breaking through the veil of the flesh for a moment. Moses stands for the Law and Elijah for the Prophets, and both of them met God on a mountain in a cloud, Moses on Sinai in Exodus 24 where "the glory of the LORD dwelt on Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it six days." Six days. Mark knows what he is doing.

- **A. Peter reaches for permanence and gets corrected.** "It is good that we are here. Let us make three tents." (Mark 9:5) Mark adds the pastoral aside that saves Peter from contempt: "For he did not know what to say, for they were terrified." Peter is not a fool. He is a frightened man reaching for the thing that would let him stay in the light and skip the valley. We do the same thing with a worship service, a conference, a mountaintop weekend — we try to pitch a tent on the feeling and never come down. And a cloud overshadows him, and the Father says the only word that matters: "This is my beloved Son; listen to him." (Mark 9:7) Not build for him. Not stay with him. Listen to him — and the last thing the Son had said was that he must suffer and die.
- **B. Elijah has already come, and they did to him whatever they pleased.** Coming down, Jesus binds glory to suffering again. They ask about Elijah, and Jesus answers that Elijah has come already, and "they did to him whatever they pleased, as it is written of him" (Mark 9:13) — John the Baptist, dead in Herod's dungeon. The forerunner of glory was a headless prisoner. Peter, on his own mountain years later, would finally understand, and write that "we were eyewitnesses of his majesty" who "heard this very voice borne from heaven" (2 Peter 1:16-18). But he learned it downhill. He learned it after the cross.

### II. The Valley That Waits at the Bottom (Mark 9:14-50)

They come down into an argument. This is the shape of the whole chapter, and it is the shape of discipleship: what is confirmed on the summit must be worked out in the dust. At the foot of the mountain is a father with a mute, convulsing boy, a knot of disciples who could not cast the demon out, and scribes disputing with them. The glory of God is on the mountain. The failure of the church is in the valley. And Jesus walks straight into the valley.

"I believe; help my unbelief." (Mark 9:24) That is the truest prayer in the Gospel, and it is a father's prayer over a broken son. The man does not pretend to more faith than he has. He brings the little he has and confesses the emptiness under it, and Jesus does not despise the confession — he heals the boy. Then, privately, the disciples ask why they failed, and Jesus answers, "This kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer" (Mark 9:29) — not by technique, not by the residue of a borrowed authority, but by the constant dependence they had let lapse.

- **A. The second passion prediction lands on deaf ears.** For the second time Jesus says plainly, "The Son of Man is going to be delivered into the hands of men, and they will kill him, and when he is killed, after three days he will rise" (Mark 9:31). And Mark records the response with unbearable honesty: "But they did not understand the saying, and were afraid to ask him." Then, on the road, they argue about which of them is greatest. They have just been told their Lord is going to be executed, and they are jockeying for cabinet positions in a kingdom that runs on crucifixion. The distance between the Father's word on the mountain and the disciples' hearts in the road is the whole problem of the human being.
- **B. Greatness is redefined by a child in the arms.** "If anyone would be first, he must be last of all and servant of all." (Mark 9:35) Then he takes a child — not a symbol of innocence to a first-century mind but a symbol of insignificance, a person with no status, no power, nothing to trade — and he puts the child in the middle and takes it in his arms. This is *diakonos*, servant, the word that will become a ransom in the next chapter. The rest of the discourse is Jesus turning the knife: better a millstone than to cause one of these little ones to sin, better to lose a hand or an eye than to be thrown whole into hell, "where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched" — Isaiah 66:24, the last verse of Isaiah, quoted over people arguing about their own greatness. Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another. The ambition that eats a fellowship is not a small thing. It is the thing Jesus warns about with the language of hell.

### III. The Tents We Still Pitch (Living Well When the Church Loves the Mountain)

Here is where I have to stop describing the disciples and turn around, because I have preached the mountain and skipped the valley, and so have you. We have built an entire Christianity around the transfiguration and quietly deleted verse 35. We want the summit experience — the retreat high, the goosebumps in the worship set, the conference where everything finally made sense — and we resist the descent into the ordinary valley where an actual broken family is waiting and the church could not help them. We have made faith a thing that happens on mountains. Jesus made it a thing that happens in dust, with a child in your arms and your own greatness left at the bottom of the hill.

Watch the machinery of it in our own history. In 1934, as the German church divided, most of it chose the mountain — the grand cathedral of national glory, the flags, the sense of a chosen people restored to greatness. A small remnant signed the Barmen Declaration in May of that year and insisted that the church listens to one Word, Jesus Christ, and to no other lord. Barmen was a valley document. It cost its signers their pulpits and, for some, their lives. The majority church kept its mountain and lost its soul, and the confessing minority came down into the dust and kept its Savior. The temptation is never as crude as idolatry. It is always the offer to stay in the light and skip the cost.

- **A. The child in the middle is the test, not the sermon.** Ambition rarely feels like ambition while you are doing it. It feels like calling. It feels like stewardship of your gifts. It feels like a healthy desire to be used. And then a person with nothing to offer walks into the room, and you find out whether you would take that person in your arms or step past them toward someone more useful. The Father said listen to him. He said it over a Son on his way to be last of all. There is no version of following that Son that ends with you first.
- **B. Christ is the one who came down for good.** The glory Peter saw on the mountain was real, and it was always his — "who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant" (Philippians 2:6-7). He did not pitch a tent on the mountain. He came down into the valley, took the broken and the convulsing and the dead into his arms, and then went further down, to a hill outside the city where the glory was hidden entirely under blood. He is the servant of all because he was first of all and refused to hold it. Listen to him.

There is a mercy in this that we miss when we are busy resenting the descent. The Father did not give Peter the vision on the mountain to torment him with a glory he would have to leave behind. He gave it so that when the valley came — the failure at the bottom of the hill, the incomprehension on the road, and finally the darkness of Golgotha — Peter would have seen, once, what was true underneath it all. The glory was real. The suffering did not cancel it. The Son who died was the Son whose clothes shone whiter than any bleach on earth. We are given our mountains for the same reason: not to live on, but to remember from, when the valley is long and the dust is deep and the child in our arms has nothing to give. The command was never "stay." The command was "listen to him," and follow.

He came down the mountain to die. Will you follow him down?

## A Ransom for Many: The Cost of the Servant King in Mark 10:17-52
*Everyone in this chapter wants a throne; only one man knows what a throne costs*

**Text:** Mark 10:17-52 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 53:10-11; 1 Timothy 2:5-6; Philippians 3:7-8; Mark 8:36-37; Matthew 20:28

Three men come to Jesus in this chapter, and all three want the same thing, though only the last one knows it. A rich man wants eternal life and will not pay for it. Two disciples want glory and do not understand the price. A blind beggar wants mercy and has nothing to lose. And between the request of the ambitious and the cry of the beggar, Jesus says the sentence the whole Gospel of Mark has been climbing toward — that he did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many. This is the center of the book. This is the center of everything.

Notice the order Mark chose, because it is not accidental. A man with everything walks away with nothing. Then men who have left everything argue about who gets the most. Then a man with nothing receives everything. The chapter is arranged as a descending and ascending line, and the pivot at the bottom of it is a cross. Mark is not stringing together three unrelated encounters. He is showing us, three times over, that the kingdom runs on an economy the world cannot compute — that the way up is down, that the price of life is death, and that the King himself is the one who pays it. Everyone in this chapter is reaching for a throne. Only one man on the road knows what a throne costs, and he is walking ahead of them toward it.

### I. The Man Who Went Away Sorrowful (Mark 10:17-31)

A man runs up and kneels — Mark's detail, the eager posture of a sincere seeker — and asks, "Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?" (Mark 10:17) It is a real question from a good man. He has kept the commandments from his youth, and Mark records the most tender line in the Gospel: "And Jesus, looking at him, loved him." (Mark 10:21) This is not a trap sprung on an enemy. This is love telling the truth at cost. "You lack one thing: go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me."

And he went away sorrowful, "for he had great possessions." He did not go away angry. He went away grieving, because he wanted eternal life and he wanted his wealth more, and for the first time in his careful, commandment-keeping life he had been shown the one god he would not surrender. Jesus did not require this of everyone he met. He required it of this man because this was the man's idol, and love goes for the idol every time.

- **A. The idol is always the thing you cannot imagine losing.** Jesus turns to the disciples: "How difficult it will be for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God." (Mark 10:23) They are amazed, because their whole world assumed wealth was a sign of God's favor. Then comes the camel and the needle's eye, and the disciples ask the honest question — "Then who can be saved?" — and Jesus lifts the whole scene into grace: "With man it is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God." (Mark 10:27) No one buys their way in. Not the rich man, not the poor. Salvation is a gift from God or it is nothing.
- **B. What is surrendered is returned a hundredfold, with persecutions.** Peter, ever the accountant, protests that they have left everything. Jesus does not scold him. He promises houses and brothers and mothers and children "now in this time," and then, without softening it, "with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life." (Mark 10:30) The hundredfold and the persecution come in the same clause. This is not the prosperity gospel and it is not the gospel of grim renunciation. It is the truth that what you give to Christ you receive back transfigured — a family, a home, a life — and a cross to carry through it. "What does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul?" (Mark 8:36) The rich man did the math wrong. We usually do.

### II. The Sons Who Asked for Thrones (Mark 10:32-45)

They are on the road going up to Jerusalem, and Mark writes that Jesus was walking ahead of them, "and they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid." (Mark 10:32) He walks toward his own execution with a stride that terrifies the people behind him. And for the third time he tells them exactly what is coming — mocked, spit upon, flogged, killed, and after three days risen — the most detailed passion prediction yet.

Their response is the request of James and John: "Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory." (Mark 10:37) He has just described his own torture, and they are asking for the two best seats. The other ten are indignant, not because the request was wrong but because James and John asked first. Every one of them wanted the throne. And Jesus gathers them and overturns the entire architecture of greatness.

- **A. Gentile greatness lords it over; kingdom greatness kneels.** "You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant." (Mark 10:42-44) The word is *diakonos*, and beneath it *doulos*, slave. This is not a management style. It is a reversal of the pyramid the whole world is built on. In the kingdom, the arrow of power points down.
- **B. The verdict the whole Gospel was built to say.** "For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many." (Mark 10:45) *Lutron anti pollōn* — a ransom in the place of many. A ransom is the price paid to free a slave or a captive; *anti* means in the place of, in exchange for, a substitution.
