Isaiah had seen it seven centuries before: "when his soul makes an offering for guilt... the righteous one, my servant, shall make many to be accounted righteous, and he shall bear their iniquities." (Isaiah 53:10-11) Paul would compress it: "who gave himself as a ransom for all" (1 Timothy 2:6). The Servant King does not merely model service. He pays the price no rich man could raise and no disciple could earn. He buys his people back with his life. Hold the two halves of the verse together and do not let anyone separate them. The first half — "not to be served but to serve" — is the ethic; it is the pattern for greatness Jesus has just laid on the disciples. The second half — "to give his life as a ransom" — is the gospel; it is a thing only he can do, a price only his blood can pay. Cut the first half loose and you get a Christianity of self-improvement, a Jesus who is only an example of humility. Cut the second half loose and you get a Jesus who purchases you but never touches how you treat the person beside you. Mark welds them in one sentence. The example flows out of the atonement, and the atonement is what the example was always pointing at. He served us all the way to the cross so that we, ransomed, would spend our lives serving each other.

### III. Which Man Are You (Living Well Among People Who Still Want the Throne)

I have to turn the mirror now, because I recognize all three men, and so do you. I have been the rich man, keeping the rules and quietly refusing the one surrender that would cost me the thing I actually worship. I have been James and John, asking Jesus to bless my ambition and calling it a desire to serve. The chapter is not about three strangers. It is a diagnostic, and every one of us fails at least two of the three. We want eternal life without releasing our grip. We want greatness without the towel and the basin. We want the crown and we skip the ransom.

Consider what our own tradition has done with this text. For centuries the American church read Mark 10:45 aloud in sanctuaries while the wealth in the pews was built, in part, on people who were themselves ransomed at auction — bought and sold as property. In 1845 the Southern Baptist Convention split from the North precisely to defend the right of missionaries to own slaves. The very people entrusted with the doctrine of the ransom held other human beings as goods to be served by. We preached the Servant who gave his life to free captives, and we made captives. This is not ancient history pointing a finger at strangers. It is my own denominational family, and it is the permanent temptation of every church that loves the throne more than the towel — to keep the words of the ransom and refuse its shape.

- **A. Greatness feels like calling right up until the towel comes out.** Nobody wants the seats at the right and the left because they are wicked. They want them because ambition wears the mask of stewardship, of vision, of using your gifts for God. The test is never the sermon you preach about service. The test is the basin. It is the person who can do nothing for you. It is the surrender you keep negotiating around. And love, looking at you, will name it — because love always goes for the idol.
- **B. The beggar shows us the only posture that works.** The chapter ends with Bartimaeus, blind, throwing off his cloak and crying, "Have mercy on me." He has no wealth to renounce and no throne to request. He has only need, and he brings it. Jesus asks him the same question he asked James and John — "What do you want me to do for you?" — but where they asked for glory, Bartimaeus asks for mercy, and receives sight, and follows Jesus on the way. The way leads to the cross. The Servant King is walking ahead of us toward it even now, and the only ones who make it up the road are the ones who came empty-handed and let him pay.

He came to give his life. Stop trying to earn what he already bought.

## The King Enters and the Tenants Are Judged: Mark 11:1-12:44
*The awaited stone arrives at the house that was built to reject him*

**Text:** Mark 11:1-12:44 · **Supporting:** Psalm 118:22-23; Isaiah 5:1-7; Jeremiah 7:11; Zechariah 9:9; Psalm 110:1

The King finally comes to His own house, and His own house has been rented out to men who mean to keep it. That is the story of these two chapters — an entrance, a cursed tree, a cleansed temple, and a parable that names the crime out loud. Jesus rides into Jerusalem as the awaited king, and within days the men who run the temple decide he must die, and they never once suspect that in deciding it they are fulfilling the very Scripture they have memorized. The rejected stone. They are the builders. And they are about to throw away the cornerstone.

For ten chapters Mark has kept a secret. Jesus silenced the demons who named him, told the healed to stay quiet, and forbade the disciples to publish his identity — the theme scholars call the messianic secret. That reticence ends at the gate of Jerusalem. The King who hid himself in Galilee now stages a public, deliberate, prophetic entrance into the capital, riding the animal Zechariah named, accepting the shouts of a crowd, and walking straight into the temple to inspect it. The secret is over because the hour has come. He is no longer preventing the confrontation. He is provoking it. And everything in these two chapters — the tree, the tables, the parable, the traps, the widow — is the collision between the true owner of the house and the tenants who forgot it was never theirs.

### I. The King Who Enters and Inspects (Mark 11:1-25)

He comes riding a colt, and Mark expects us to hear Zechariah under it: "Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey." (Zechariah 9:9) The crowds spread cloaks and shout "Hosanna" — save now — and they are right about the words and wrong about the king. They want a conqueror who will drive out Rome. He has come to drive out the money-changers. Then Mark records something strange: the King enters the temple, "looked around at everything," and, "as it was already late, he went out to Bethany." (Mark 11:11) He inspects the house and leaves. The judgment is already forming.

The next morning he curses a fig tree in full leaf but bearing no fruit, and Mark wraps the temple cleansing inside the story of that tree — a technique scholars call intercalation, one story split to interpret another. The fig tree is the temple. Leaves without fruit. The show of religion without the reality of it.

- **A. A house of prayer made a den of robbers.** He drives out the sellers, overturns the tables, and quotes two prophets at once: "My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations. But you have made it a den of robbers." (Mark 11:17) That second line is Jeremiah 7:11, spoken just before the first temple was destroyed in 586 BC. Jesus is not merely cleaning up a market. He is standing in the temple, quoting the sermon that preceded the last time God let this house fall, and telling them it is happening again. "A house of prayer for all the nations" — and they had turned the one court where Gentiles could pray into a livestock exchange. The house built to welcome the nations had become a business that excluded them.
- **B. The withered tree is the verdict on fruitless religion.** In the morning the fig tree has withered to its roots, and Jesus turns it into a lesson on faith and forgiveness — "whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it" (Mark 11:24). But the frame is unmistakable. The temple, like the tree, had leaves and no fruit, and its time was ending. Religion that performs and does not bear — that keeps the liturgy and loses the love, that runs the machinery and forgets the poor — is a tree in full leaf on the day the King comes hungry.

### II. The Tenants Who Killed the Heir (Mark 11:27-12:44)

The authorities confront him: "By what authority are you doing these things?" (Mark 11:28) He answers a question with a question about John's baptism, traps them in their own cowardice, and then tells a parable that leaves nothing hidden. A man plants a vineyard, lets it out to tenants, and goes away. This is Isaiah 5 word for word — "the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel" (Isaiah 5:7) — and every listener knew it. The owner sends servants for the fruit; the tenants beat and kill them, one after another. The servants are the prophets.

"He had still one other, a beloved son. Finally he sent him to them, saying, 'They will respect my son.' But those tenants said to one another, 'This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.'" (Mark 12:6-7) He is telling them, to their faces, that they are the tenants, that he is the son, and that they are about to kill him — and that they will do it precisely because they know who he is. This is the terrible clarity of the parable. They do not reject the heir out of ignorance. They reject him because they recognize him and want the vineyard for themselves.

- **A. The rejected stone becomes the cornerstone.** Then Jesus quotes the psalm the whole scene turns on: "The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. This was the Lord's doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes." (Mark 12:10-11, from Psalm 118:22-23) The builders — the professionals, the experts, the men whose job is to know which stone belongs — examine the cornerstone and discard it as worthless. And God takes the stone they threw away and makes it the foundation of everything. Peter would later throw this verse at the same council that condemned Jesus. The men best qualified to recognize the Messiah were the ones who killed him, and their rejection became the doing of the Lord.
- **B. Every trap is turned, and one widow tells the truth.** The rest of chapter 12 is a series of tests — taxes to Caesar, the resurrection, the great commandment — and Jesus turns each one, ending with his own question from Psalm 110:1: how can the Christ be David's son when David calls him Lord? Then, after all the theology, Mark closes with a widow. She puts in two small coins, "everything she had, all she had to live on." (Mark 12:44) The tenants held the whole vineyard and gave the owner nothing. The widow held two coins and gave God everything. That is the contrast the chapter was built to make. The temple full of leaves, and one woman bearing fruit.

### III. The Vineyard We Still Try to Keep (Living Well as Tenants Who Forget the Owner)

I cannot preach this parable at the Pharisees and walk away clean, and neither can you, because the tenants' sin is not exotic. It is the oldest sin in the church: to be entrusted with something that belongs to God and to begin, slowly, to treat it as ours. The pulpit becomes my platform. The congregation becomes my achievement. The gifts become my property. And when the true owner sends word asking for fruit — asking whether the poor are fed, whether the nations are welcomed, whether the house is still a house of prayer — we send the messenger away, because we have grown used to keeping the vineyard for ourselves. The builders rejected the stone because they had forgotten they were only builders. The house was never theirs.

The pattern runs straight through Christian history. Consider the church of the fourth century after Constantine's Edict of Milan in 313 and Theodosius making Nicene Christianity the empire's official religion in 380 — the moment the persecuted movement of the catacombs inherited the vineyard and, within a few generations, began to run it like the empire it had replaced, complete with power, property, and the machinery of exclusion. Every time the church has been handed the vineyard — cultural power, political favor, a Christian nation — it has been tempted to kill the messengers who ask for fruit and to keep the inheritance for itself. The temptation is never to become pagan. It is to keep the temple and forget the One greater than the temple standing in it.

- **A. Fruitlessness rarely feels like rebellion. It feels like management.** The tenants were not lazy. They were running the vineyard — pruning, harvesting, defending the property. They were busy. That is what makes the parable so exact. You can be furiously active in the work of God and be, in fact, keeping God's vineyard from God. The question the owner sends is always the same and always unwelcome: where is the fruit that belongs to me?
- **B. The stone you reject is the only foundation you have.** Here is the mercy hidden in the judgment. The stone the builders threw away God did not destroy — he made it the cornerstone. The rejected Christ is the rejected Christ still on offer, still the only foundation on which anything holds. The King who entered Jerusalem to be killed entered knowing he would be the stone they discarded, and knowing that his rejection would become, by the Lord's doing, the salvation of the very builders who threw him away. The house is still his. He is still asking for fruit. And the cornerstone is still the one you keep trying to build without.

And notice how the two chapters end — not with the parable's judgment, but with a widow's coin. After the tenants who kept everything and gave nothing, Mark shows us a poor woman who kept nothing and gave everything, and Jesus calls his disciples over specifically to see her. She is the anti-tenant. She is what the vineyard was supposed to produce. The judgment on the fruitless temple and the commendation of the fruitful widow stand in the same chapter, because the alternative to being a tenant who hoards is not despair — it is the widow who, holding two coins over a treasury that had failed everyone like her, still gave them to God. The cornerstone the builders rejected is the same cornerstone she was, in her two small coins, building her whole life upon. The judgment names what we have done with the vineyard. The widow shows what a ransomed heart does with everything it has left.

The builders rejected him. God made him the foundation.

## Watch: The One Command That Outlasts the Temple in Mark 13:1-37
*The buildings you admire will fall; the question is whether you are awake when they do*

**Text:** Mark 13:1-37 · **Supporting:** Daniel 7:13-14; Daniel 9:27; 2 Peter 3:3-4; 1 Thessalonians 5:2-6; Isaiah 13:10

A disciple points at the temple like a tourist — "Look, Teacher, what wonderful stones and what wonderful buildings" — and Jesus answers by telling him that not one of those stones will be left on another. That is how this chapter begins, with a man admiring a building that is already condemned. And the whole discourse that follows, dense and disputed and full of clouds and stars falling, presses down to a single word repeated to the end. Not a date. Not a chart. A command. Stay awake. Because the thing you were admiring is going to fall, and the only question that matters is whether you will be found watching or sleeping when it does.

More sermons have been wrecked on this chapter than perhaps any other, because we come to it asking the disciples' question — when, and what is the sign — and Jesus refuses to answer it and answers a different question instead. He will not give us the timetable. He gives us the posture. Whole libraries have been written mapping the wars and the abominations and the darkened sun onto the newspaper, and every generation has been sure it was the last, and every generation has been wrong about the calendar and right about the summons. Because the summons never expires. The chapter is not a code to be cracked. It is a command to be obeyed, and the command is the same whether the end comes tomorrow or in a thousand years. Watch. Stay awake. You do not know the hour, and the not-knowing is the point.

### I. The Buildings That Will Not Stand (Mark 13:1-23)

"Do you see these great buildings? There will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down." (Mark 13:2) In the year 70, within the lifetime of some who heard him, the Roman legions under Titus burned the temple to the ground and pulled it apart stone by stone. Jesus is not speaking in vague apocalypse. He is predicting a specific catastrophe that specific people would live to see. The disciples ask, privately, "when will these things be, and what will be the sign?" (Mark 13:4) — and Jesus refuses to give them the timetable they want and gives them instead a posture.

The first word out of his mouth is a warning against deception. "See that no one leads you astray. Many will come in my name, saying, 'I am he,' and they will lead many astray." (Mark 13:5-6) Then wars, earthquakes, famines — and the pastoral clause we skip: "This must take place, but the end is not yet. These are but the beginning of the birth pains." (Mark 13:7-8) He is telling them, in advance, not to read every crisis as the finale. The world will be full of alarming signs, and most of them will be labor, not delivery.

- **A. Persecution is the normal weather of the church, not the exception.** "They will deliver you over to councils, and you will be beaten in synagogues... and you will be hated by all for my name's sake. But the one who endures to the end will be saved." (Mark 13:9, 13) The word is *hupomonē* — endurance, remaining under weight. Jesus does not promise his followers an escape from tribulation. He promises them the presence of the Spirit in the dock — "do not be anxious beforehand what you are to say... for it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit" (Mark 13:11) — and the strength to remain under the weight to the end. Endurance, not evacuation, is the shape of faithfulness.
- **B. The abomination and the flight from Judea.** Then a hinge: "when you see the abomination of desolation standing where he ought not to be... then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains." (Mark 13:14) The phrase comes from Daniel 9:27, and Mark adds a wink to the reader — "let the reader understand." History records that Jerusalem's Christians, remembering this warning, fled the city before the siege closed. The words that sounded like riddles were, for the people who took them seriously, the instructions that saved their lives. Jesus tells his people the truth about the fall so that they will not be sleeping when it comes.

### II. The Son of Man on the Clouds (Mark 13:24-37)

Beyond the fall of the temple, the discourse lifts to something larger. "The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will be falling from heaven." (Mark 13:24-25) This is the language of Isaiah 13, the prophetic idiom for the collapse of a world order, and it points past 70 AD to the end itself. "And then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory." (Mark 13:26) That is Daniel 7:13 — "one like a son of man" coming with the clouds of heaven, to whom is given "dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him." (Daniel 7:14) The one on trial before the council will soon claim exactly this title, and it will be counted blasphemy.

Then the lesson of the fig tree, reversed from chapter 11 — when its branch is tender and the leaves come out, summer is near — and the promise that "this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away." (Mark 13:30-31) The temple will fall in their generation, a guaranteed proof; the greater day is certain because his word does not fail.

- **A. No one knows the day — not even the Son.** "But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father." (Mark 13:32) This is the verse that ends all date-setting. If the Son himself, in his incarnate mission, did not hold the calendar, then every man who has ever named the year has claimed to know what Christ did not. The point of the not-knowing is not despair. It is vigilance. Ignorance of the hour is precisely what makes every hour the hour to be ready.
- **B. The command that carries the whole chapter: watch.** The discourse ends with a parable of a master who leaves home, puts his servants in charge, "and commands the doorkeeper to stay awake." (Mark 13:34) "Therefore stay awake — for you do not know when the master of the house will come... lest he come suddenly and find you asleep. And what I say to you I say to all: Stay awake." (Mark 13:35-37) Four times in the closing lines: watch, stay awake, keep watch. The entire towering discourse of temples and tribulation and the Son of Man on the clouds collapses into one imperative aimed at the ordinary servant on an ordinary night. Be awake. Be at your post. He is coming, and he did not tell you when.

### III. The Buildings We Still Admire (Living Well While Awake in a Sleeping Age)

I have to turn this on us, because I am the disciple pointing at the wonderful buildings. So are you. We admire the institutions we have built — the growing church, the influential ministry, the Christian culture, the political power we imagine will secure the faith — and we say, look, Teacher, what wonderful stones. And the answer is the same. Not one of them will be left standing. Everything you can point to and admire is temporary, and the only thing that endures is the Word that does not pass away and the Master who is coming back. To live well is to hold every visible thing loosely and to stay awake for the one thing that lasts.

The command to watch is the command we are worst at, and the reason is not that we deny Christ will return — it is that we get bored waiting. Peter named it in the first century: "scoffers will come... saying, 'Where is the promise of his coming? For ever since the fathers fell asleep, all things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation.'" (2 Peter 3:3-4) The danger is not primarily the false messiah with the loud claim. It is the slow anesthesia of a world where nothing seems to happen, where the master delays, where the servant decides the return is theoretical and goes to sleep at his post. The Millerites set October 22, 1844, and when the Lord did not come they called it the Great Disappointment — and the deeper disappointment of the church has never been the wrong date. It has been the servant who stopped watching because the right date never came. Paul's word stands: "you are not in darkness... So then let us not sleep, as others do, but let us keep awake and be sober." (1 Thessalonians 5:4-6)

- **A. Sleep does not feel like sleep. It feels like normal life.** The servant who falls asleep at his post does not decide to betray the master. He just gets comfortable. The waiting stretches on, the crisis never arrives, the ordinary days accumulate, and vigilance quietly relaxes into routine until the return that was always certain becomes, in practice, forgotten. That is why the command is repeated four times. Watchfulness is not a mood you summon in an emergency. It is a discipline you keep on the ordinary night, when nothing is happening and everything is at stake.
- **B. The One who commands the watch has already kept it for us.** The Son who did not know the hour is the same Son who, a chapter later, would stay awake in Gethsemane while his disciples slept, who would watch and pray through the night his own return-in-glory was purchased. He commands us to keep watch because he kept it first, alone, when the ones told to watch with him could not stay awake one hour. Read the two scenes side by side, because Mark meant them to be read that way. Here in chapter 13 the command is "stay awake." In chapter 14 the same word comes to Peter, James, and John in the garden — "Remain here and watch" — and Jesus returns to find them sleeping, and says, "Could you not watch one hour?" The men who received the command to watch could not keep it for a single hour on the night it mattered most. And the Son kept it for them, awake and in agony, sweating out the cup while they slept. He is coming on the clouds with power and glory — and he is coming for servants he will find at their posts, sober, awake, holding the temporary things loosely and the eternal Word tight. The one who commands your vigilance already paid for your sleeping.

Stay awake. You do not know the hour.

## The Cross of the Servant King: Betrayal, Silence, and the Torn Curtain in Mark 14:1-15:47
*The One who could silence a storm chose to be silenced, and a Roman soldier said the first true thing in the whole book*

**Text:** Mark 14:1-15:47 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 53:7; Psalm 22:1; Exodus 26:31-33; Hebrews 10:19-20; Zechariah 13:7

Everything Mark has been building toward comes to this: the Servant King is arrested, tried, mocked, and killed, and every human being close to him fails. One friend sells him. One friend denies him three times. The rest run into the dark. The council condemns him and the crowd chooses a murderer over him and the soldiers gamble for his clothes while he dies. And in the middle of all this human collapse, the man himself is almost entirely silent — the one who commanded demons and stilled the sea says almost nothing, because the servant was going to give his life, and giving it meant not defending it. Then the curtain tears, and a Roman soldier who watched him die says the sentence Mark wrote in his very first verse.

### I. The Servant Who Refused to Save Himself (Mark 14:1-72)

It opens with two acts of devotion and betrayal side by side. A woman pours a year's wages of ointment over his head, and Jesus says, "She has done a beautiful thing to me... she has anointed my body beforehand for burial." (Mark 14:6, 8) She understands, in the only way anyone in this Gospel understands, that he is going to die. And in the same breath, Judas goes to the chief priests to sell him. Extravagant love and cold betrayal, framed together, because that is what will surround the cross from here on.

At the table he takes bread and a cup and says, "This is my body... This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many." (Mark 14:22-24) The ransom of chapter 10 becomes a meal. Then Gethsemane, where the man who told the storm to be still falls on the ground and prays, "Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will." (Mark 14:36) He does not want to die. He is not a Stoic marching to a noble end. He is in agony, and he drinks the cup anyway, because obedience to the Father costs exactly this. And the disciples told to watch with him fall asleep.

There is a detail here Mark will not let us romanticize. Jesus prays three times to have the cup removed, and three times the answer is no — and then, having received the Father's silence, he rises and walks toward the men coming to arrest him without a trace of hesitation. The agony was real and the obedience was total, and they were not in conflict. This is what obedience costs when it is real. Not the absence of dread, but the presence of surrender inside the dread. The Servant King did not want to die. He wanted the Father's will more, and the two wants met in a garden at night and the deeper want won.

- **A. The trial where silence was the sermon.** At the council the false witnesses cannot agree, and Jesus says nothing. "But he remained silent and made no answer." (Mark 14:61) Isaiah had seen it: "like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth." (Isaiah 53:7) The man who out-argued every trap in the temple courts stands before his accusers and does not defend himself. He breaks the silence only once, when the high priest asks directly, "Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?" And Jesus says, "I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven." (Mark 14:62) It is Daniel 7 and Psalm 110 out of the mouth of the accused. He answers with a claim to the throne, and they answer with a verdict of death.
- **B. The friend who cursed and wept.** While Jesus confesses upstairs, Peter denies downstairs — three times, the last with curses — and then the rooster crows, and "he broke down and wept." (Mark 14:72) Zechariah had foretold it: "Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered." (Zechariah 13:7) The strongest disciple, the one who swore he would die first, discovers in a courtyard that he is made of the same failing material as the rest of us. This is not a footnote. Mark puts Peter's collapse next to Jesus' confession on purpose. The Servant is faithful precisely where his people are not.

### II. The Death That Tore the Veil (Mark 15:1-47)

Pilate finds no case and yields to the crowd anyway, washing his hands of a man he knows is innocent, releasing Barabbas — a genuine insurrectionist and murderer — in the place of the innocent one. The substitution is acted out in the street before it is accomplished on the cross: the guilty man goes free because the innocent man takes his place. Then the soldiers dress Jesus in purple, crown him with thorns, and kneel in mockery — "Hail, King of the Jews" — not knowing that every word of their cruelty is true.

They crucify him at the third hour, between two robbers, and hang a placard over his head: "The King of the Jews." (Mark 15:26) The mockery continues — "He saved others; he cannot save himself. Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross, that we may see and believe." (Mark 15:31-32) And here is the terrible center of the Gospel. He could have come down. The power that raised a dead girl and stilled the sea was intact. He does not save himself, because he cannot save himself and save us both, and he chose us. The taunt is the truest theology in the chapter, spoken by men who did not know they were preaching.

- **A. The cry of dereliction.** At the ninth hour he cries with a loud voice, "Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?" — "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Mark 15:34) It is the first line of Psalm 22, and it is not a moment of lost faith — the man still says "my God" — but it is real forsakenness. The Son who had known unbroken communion with the Father from eternity drinks the cup to its dregs, and the cup is this: to bear the sin of many is to bear the God-forsakenness that sin earns. This is the ransom being paid. Not a symbol. A Son crying into a silent heaven so that we would never have to.
- **B. The curtain torn and the centurion's confession.** "And Jesus uttered a loud cry and breathed his last. And the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom." (Mark 15:37-38) The veil of Exodus 26 that walled off the Holy of Holies, the barrier between God and the people, is ripped — and torn from the top, by a hand no man could reach. Hebrews would name it: "we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh." (Hebrews 10:19-20) And then the last confession: a Roman centurion, the man who ran the execution, watching how Jesus died, says, "Truly this man was the Son of God." (Mark 15:39) Mark opened his book, "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." The first human being in the entire Gospel to say it plainly and rightly is a pagan soldier standing at the foot of a cross. Not Peter. Not the twelve. A Gentile executioner, looking at a dead man, sees what the insiders missed.

### III. The Cross We Still Want Without the Weight (Living Well Under a Servant Who Would Not Come Down)

I have to stand under this cross honestly, and so do you, because we love the torn curtain and we skip the forsaken cry. We want the access without the abandonment, the open way without the God-forsaken Son who opened it. We want a Jesus who saves others and also saves himself, who wins without losing, who reigns without the nails. And that Jesus does not exist. The whole point of Mark 15 is that he would not come down. The mockers offered him the one thing our flesh always wants — save yourself, prove your power, refuse the humiliation — and he refused it, because coming down would have left us in the tomb. Every time we ask God for a faith that costs us nothing, we are the crowd at the foot of the cross, asking him to come down.

Watch how the church forgets this. In Germany in the 1930s, the Deutsche Christen — the German Christian movement — wanted a strong Christ, a victorious Christ, a Christ scrubbed of Jewish weakness and fitted to national glory. They wanted a Savior who came down from the cross. In May 1934 the Barmen Declaration, drafted largely by Karl Barth, answered that the church has one Word to hear and obey, "Jesus Christ, as he is attested for us in Holy Scripture" — the crucified one, not the conquering idol the age preferred. The permanent temptation of the church is to trade the Servant King who dies for a strong king who wins. It is always the same trade. It is always the crowd saying, come down and we will believe. And the gospel is the man who stayed on the cross so that we could enter through the veil his death tore open.

- **A. Self-saving always feels like faithfulness. It is the oldest refusal.** The temptation on the cross was the same one in the wilderness at the start of the Gospel — prove yourself, use the power, refuse the humiliating path. It never announces itself as unbelief. It comes dressed as reasonableness, as good stewardship of power, as the sensible refusal to suffer needlessly. And it is, at root, the demand that God serve us rather than the confession that the Son of Man came not to be served. The cross is the place where that demand dies.
- **B. Christ was forsaken so that you would be received.** The cry of dereliction is the hinge of the mercy. He was forsaken so that you would never hear "why have you forsaken me" and get no answer. The curtain tore from the top because you could never have torn it from the bottom, and it tore the moment he died because his death was the tearing. The centurion looked at a dead man and saw the Son of God — which means the cross is not the failure of the gospel, it is the gospel, the throne of the Servant King, the place where the ransom of chapter 10 was actually paid. He did not come down. He stayed, for you.

Truly this was the Son of God.

## He Has Risen; He Is Not Here: The Unfinished Ending of Mark 16:1-8
*The women came to anoint a corpse, found an empty tomb, and Mark hands you the ending to finish*

**Text:** Mark 16:1-8 · **Supporting:** 1 Corinthians 15:14-19; Mark 14:28; Isaiah 25:8; Romans 6:4; Mark 16:6

Mark ends the way no one would end it. No appearance of the risen Christ. No reunion in the upper room. No commissioning on a mountain. Eight verses: three women, an open tomb, a young man in white, an announcement, and then terror and silence. "And they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid." (Mark 16:8) That is the last line of the earliest text of the Gospel. The scholars debate whether Mark meant to stop there or whether the true ending was lost. But read as it stands, this abrupt, unfinished, unsatisfying ending is doing something no tidy ending could do. It leaves the reader holding the announcement the women were too afraid to carry. It hands the ending to you.

### I. The Women Who Came to Care for a Corpse (Mark 16:1-4)

They come when the Sabbath is past, at sunrise, with spices, "so that they might go and anoint him." (Mark 16:1) Read that plainly. They are not coming to a resurrection. They are coming to a funeral. They have bought ointment to tend a decomposing body, because that is what love does when hope is dead — it keeps caring for the corpse. These women watched him die when the disciples had fled. They are the last faithful, and their faithfulness is entirely aimed at the past tense. They love a dead man and they have come to do the dead man's honors.

Their only worry, on the way, is logistics: "Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?" (Mark 16:3) The stone was very large. They have thought about the ointment and the spices and the strength it will take to move a boulder they cannot budge, and they have not once considered that the tomb might be empty, because empty tombs are not a category the human mind keeps ready. And then they look up. "And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled back." (Mark 16:4) The problem they had spent the walk worrying about had already been solved by a power that had been at work while they slept.

- **A. Faithfulness to a dead Christ is still faithfulness — and still not enough.** There is something deeply moving and deeply insufficient about these women. They are more faithful than the men. They showed up. But their whole framework is grief management. They have come to make death a little more bearable, not to meet the living God, because they believed the story was over. And I recognize that faith exactly. It is the faith that admires Jesus, honors his memory, tends the tradition, and quietly assumes the tomb is still occupied. It is devotion without resurrection. It brings spices to a grave. It is possible to love Jesus sincerely, to be more faithful than the people who ran, and still to be organizing your whole spiritual life around a corpse. That is the sober warning buried in the tenderness of these women. Sincerity is not the same as resurrection faith. You can honor a dead teacher with real tears. Only a living Lord can be followed to Galilee.
- **B. The stone was moved before they arrived.** The detail matters. The stone was not rolled away so that Jesus could get out — he was already gone. It was rolled away so that they could get in and see. God does not wait for our strength to be adequate to the boulder. The obstacle that consumed their worry was removed before they ever reached it, not by their effort but by his power. They came prepared to fail at the one thing they thought they needed to do, and found it already done.

### II. The Announcement That Reverses Everything (Mark 16:5-7)

Inside sits a young man in a white robe, and the women are alarmed. And he gives them the announcement that is the hinge of history in one sentence: "Do not be alarmed. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him." (Mark 16:6) Every clause carries weight. He names the crucified Jesus — the same one, the real one, the one who died, not a spirit or a symbol. *Ēgerthē* — he was raised, a divine passive, God did this. He is not here. And then the invitation to verify: see the place. There is a specific spot where a specific body was laid, and it is empty. This is not a feeling the women had. It is an event with an address.

Then the commission: "But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you." (Mark 16:7) Two things break the heart open here. First, "and Peter" — the man who denied him three times with curses is named specifically, singled out for the good news, restored before he has done anything to earn it. The risen Christ's first recorded concern is the disciple who failed worst. Second, "he is going before you to Galilee" — exactly what Jesus had said the night he was betrayed: "But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee." (Mark 14:28) The word held. Everything the Servant King predicted has now come true, down to the last detail, including this.

- **A. The resurrection is either an event or it is nothing.** Paul would stake the entire faith on this and refuse every softer reading: "If Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain... If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied." (1 Corinthians 15:14, 19) There is no version of Christianity that survives the loss of the empty tomb. It is not a metaphor for renewal, not a symbol of hope springing eternal, not the persistence of Jesus' influence in the hearts of his followers. It is a body that was dead and is not dead, a stone rolled back on an event, and Isaiah's ancient promise finally kept: "He will swallow up death forever." (Isaiah 25:8)
- **B. He goes before you — the risen Christ is always ahead, never behind.** The women came looking backward, to a tomb, to a body, to the past. The announcement turns them around: he is not here, he is ahead of you, in Galilee, where the ordinary life is, where the fishing and the crowds and the work are. The risen Christ does not stay in the tomb to be visited. He goes before his people into the future, into the ordinary places, and there they will see him. The resurrection is not a monument to visit. It is a person who has gone on ahead and is waiting where you are going.

### III. The Ending Mark Handed to Us (Living Well as People Who Must Finish the Story)

Here is why the abrupt ending is not a flaw but the sharpest move in the book, and here is where I have to turn it on us. "They went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them, and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid." (Mark 16:8) The first witnesses of the resurrection ran away and said nothing. And there the Gospel stops, unfinished, because the announcement now has no one to carry it — except the reader holding the book. Mark has done to us exactly what the young man did to the women. He has given us the message and left us with the choice the women faced: believe the word and go, or be afraid and say nothing. The silence at the end of Mark is a space with your name on it.

I have to confess that I have lived in verse 8 more than I would like to admit. I have believed the resurrection on Sunday and been afraid to say anything about it on Monday, held the greatest announcement in human history and let fear turn me silent in the exact places it needed to be spoken. And so has the church, again and again. Consider that within three centuries this frightened, silent, fleeing beginning had reached the whole Roman world — not by power, the church had none, but because eventually the ones who fled the tomb went back and opened their mouths, and kept opening them under Nero and under Diocletian's persecution of 303, until an empire that crucified its founder confessed him Lord. The historian Tom Holland, no believer himself, argues in his 2019 book Dominion that the moral assumptions of the entire Western world were rewired by this event and its witnesses — that the very instinct to side with the victim rather than the strong descends from a crucified man walking out of a tomb. The women's fear did not get the last word. The question is whether ours will.

- **A. Fear rarely feels like unbelief. It feels like discretion.** The women did not run because they doubted the empty tomb — they had seen it. They ran because the truth was too large and too dangerous to carry, and silence felt safer than speech. That is our temptation exactly. We do not deny the resurrection. We just keep quiet about it, and we call the quiet prudence, or humility, or respect for other people's space. But the announcement was never given to be admired in private. It was given with a command attached: go, tell. An unspoken resurrection is a stone rolled back for no one.
- **B. Christ has already gone ahead; the only question is whether you follow.** The mercy in this ending is that everything depends on him and nothing on the quality of the first witnesses. They failed, and he had already gone before them to Galilee anyway. Peter denied him, and he was named first in the good news anyway. The disciples fled, and the risen Christ was waiting for them up the road regardless. The resurrection does not wait for brave witnesses. It creates them, eventually, out of frightened ones, because the tomb is empty whether or not anyone says so, and the living Christ is ahead of you in the ordinary places right now, exactly as he said. Mark hands you the pen. The tomb is open. He is going before you.

Believe the word and go.
